## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.84141.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.84141.3.sa2)

The manuscript presents a computational model of how an organism might learn a map of the structure of its environment and the location of valuable resources through synaptic plasticity, and how this map could subsequently be used for goal-directed navigation.

The model is composed of 'map cells', which learn the structure of the environment in their recurrent connections, and 'goal-cell' which store the location of valued resources with respect to the map cell population. Each map cell corresponds to a particular location in the environment due to receiving external excitatory input at this location. The synaptic plasticity rule between map cells potentiates synapses when activity above a specified threshold at the pre-synaptic neuron is followed by above-threshold activity at the post-synaptic neuron. The threshold is set such that map neurons are only driven above this plasticity threshold by the external excitatory input, causing synapses to only be potentiated between a pair of map neurons when the organism moves directly between the locations they represent. This causes the weight matrix between the map neurons to learn the adjacency for the graph of locations in the environment, i.e. after learning the synaptic weight matrix matches the environment's adjacency matrix. Recurrent activity in the map neuron population then causes a bump of activity centred on the current location, which drops off exponentially with the diffusion distance on the graph. Each goal cell receives input from the map cells, and also from a 'resource cell' whose activity indicates the presence or absence of a given values resource at the current location. Synaptic plasticity potentiates map-cell to goal-cell synapses in proportion to the activity of the map cells at time-points when the resource cell is active. This causes goal cell activity to increase when the activity of the map cell population is similar to the activity where the resource was obtained. The upshot of all this is that after learning the activity of goal cells decreases exponentially with the diffusion distance from the corresponding goal location. The organism can therefore navigate to a given goal by doing gradient ascent on the activity of the corresponding goal cell. The process of evaluating these gradients and using them to select actions is not modelled explicitly, but the authors point to the similarity of this mechanism to chemotaxis (ascending a gradient of odour concentration to reach the odour source), and the widespread capacity for chemotaxis in the animal kingdom, to argue for its biological plausibility. The ideas are interesting and the presentation of the results in the manuscript is generally clear.

Closely related ideas have been explored in previous work, and there are some aspects of how the work relates to previous literature that it would be useful to clarify. Several lines of work have proposed learning long-range relationships between states in the environment, to enable navigation to rewarding goals by effectively descending distance gradients. The most well-known of these in the neuroscience literature is the Successor Representation (SR) (Dayan 1993), which is defined as the expected discounted future occupancy of each state given the current state. As noted in the discussion, this is closely related to the representation learnt by the map cells in the current model. The key difference is that the successor representation uses state-state transitions under a given policy (a mapping from states to actions), whereas the current model uses the adjacency matrix between states, which depends only on the environment and hence is independent of the policy followed while the representation is learnt (given sufficient exploration). This policy independence is useful, as the SR can fail to generate good routes to goals when these are very different from the policy under which it was learned (see Russek et al. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005768). However, there are several prior proposals for policy-independent SR-like mechanisms that it would be useful to discuss. Baram et al. (https://doi.org/10.1101/421461) propose navigating to goals by doing gradient descent on diffusion distances, computed as powers of the adjacency matrix as in the current work. One limitation of using the adjacency matrix is that it does not handle situations where transitions between states are probabilistic, which is not a big issue for navigation in physical space but is for applying the mechanism to cognitive tasks more broadly. There are prior ideas for learning policy-independent representations similar to the SR that do not have this limitation. Kaelbling (Learning to achieve goals, IJCAI, 1993) proposed using an off-policy learning rule similar to Q-learning, to learn shortest path distances between states. Piray and Daw (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25123-3) consider a default representation, which is a successor-like representation under a generic default policy, building on the Linear Markov Decision Process (LMDP) framework of Todorov (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0710743106). Also relevant to the current study is the work of Fang et al. (https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.80680) who, as in the current work, propose using recurrent network dynamics to compute a long-range representation (the SR) from synaptic weights that store local transition information.

One other area where I felt the work could be better integrated with the existing literature was the discussion of mapping the model onto brain circuits. An interesting and attractive aspect of the work is the idea that the relatively high-level operation of goal-directed navigation could be built on top of evolutionarily older mechanisms for ascending odour gradients. Given this framing, I was expecting the discussion of brain circuits to consider interactions between spatial mapping systems and regions involved in olfactory processing. However the discussion of mammalian brains focussed exclusively on the hippocampus without any link to olfaction, which feels like a missed opportunity. I am not an expert on olfaction, but one region that seems particularly interesting in this context is the olfactory tubercle (see Wesson & Wilson https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2010.08.004 for a review). This region is contiguous with the ventral striatum and has similar local circuitry, receives strong input from olfactory regions, but also input from the hippocampal formation, and a strong dopaminergic innervation from VTA. This suggests a mapping of the model to brain circuits in which map cells in the hippocampal formation project to goal cells in the olfactory tubercle, with the dopaminergic input acting as resource cells (note that different dopamine neuron populations appear to respond to different reward types, see e.g. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04954-0, https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.05.09.540067). I was also surprised not to see any discussion of internally generated sequential activity in the hippocampus as a possible mechanism for the look-ahead needed to evaluate the goal distance gradient, particularly given the authors suggest that vicarious trial and error (VTE) is a behavioural signature of this gradient sampling, and it is known that during VTE hippocampus plays out internally generated sequences of possible future locations (see Redish https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn.2015.30).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.84141.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.84141.3.sa3)

This paper describes an algorithm that provides a general mechanism for goal-directed behaviour in a biologically plausible neural form.

The method depends on substantial simplifying assumptions. The simulated animal effectively moves through an environment consisting of discrete locations and can reliably detect when it is in each location. Whenever it moves from one location to an adjacent location, it perfectly learns the connectivity between these two locations (changes the value in an adjacency matrix to 1). This creates a graph of connections that reflects the explored environment. In this graph, the current location gets input activation and this spreads to all connected nodes multiplied by a constant decay (adjusted to the branching number of the graph) so that as the number of connection steps increases the activation decreases. Some locations will be marked as goals through experiencing a resource of a specific identity there and subsequently will be activated by an amount proportional to their distance in the graph from the current location, i.e., their activation will increase if the agent moves a step closer and decrease if it moves a step further away. Hence by making such exploratory movements, the animal can decide which way to move to obtain a specified goal.

Although the algorithm is presented within a conceptual framework of chemotaxis, I.e., making movements to sample a local gradient and move up it, the approach relates closely to previous models of exploration, learning, and navigation that similarly establish (through experience) a graph structure to represent how locations are connected and use some form of activity-propagation from the current node or goal node to identify a (shortest) route between them. Many of these similarly claim to be plausible neural circuits. The current authors argue that the current algorithm has several desirable features with respect to such previous work: for example, the 'readout' of the path does not require explicit 'look-up' and activation of the goal node (although it does require a choice of which goal node is currently connected to behavior); and does not require any separate control or rules for learning vs. navigation phases. By comparison to the successor representation method used in RL, which also appears related, they note that the gain (decay) factor is not equivalent to a temporal discount and that their method learns only state-state transitions, allowing the value of actions to be externalised, I.e., calculated by trying alternative actions to see which increases the activation at the goal node the most. On the other hand, it should be noted that some issues addressed in previous models, such as uncertainty over the current state or probabilistic state(-action) transitions are not addressed in this work.

The algorithm presents some elegant features with respect to previous work such as conceptually separating the 'goal' nodes from the state (location) graph (I.e. 'goals' are not just special target states within the graph) so that a small number of goals can become associated to (potentially) multiple regions of the state graph where they are satisfied, or near to being satisfied. This architecture is suggested, in the discussion, to resemble the insect mushroom body (MB), where it is known that a small number of output neurons (MBONs, putative goal neurons) are activated by plastic connections from Kenyon cells (KCs, putative state neurons). However, it goes substantially beyond any available evidence to claim that KC connectivity could support the acquisition of a graph (in the form of an adjacency matrix) representing the structure of the environment: KCs show sparse distributed activity (not one active node per state); it seems unlikely that any two arbitrary KCs can (rapidly) become connected; and as yet has not been demonstrated that KC connectivity is plastic at all.

The results presented are fairly straightforward given the simplification of the tasks, as described above. They show (1) in practical terms, the spreading signal travels further for a larger decay but becomes erratic as the decay parameter (map neuron gain) approaches its theoretical upper bound and decreases below noise levels beyond a certain distance. Both follow the theory but it is perhaps helpful to see that there is a viable range of values of the gain for which the mechanism works, that is, it is not highly dependent on precise tuning. (2) That different graph structures can be acquired and used to approach goal locations (not surprising). (3) That simultaneous learning and exploitation of the graph only minimally affects the performance over starting with perfect knowledge of the graph. (4) That the parameters interact in expected ways. (5) That the separation of goals from states can be used flexibly e.g. the homing behaviour (a goal state is learned before any of the map is learned) and the patrolling behaviour (a goal cell that monitors all states for how recently they were visited). It is also interesting to link the mechanism of exploration of neighbouring states to observed scanning behaviours in navigating animals. It would have been interesting to explore whether the parameters could be dynamically tuned, based on the overall graph activity.

results.result: The endotaxis algorithm is implemented as a 3-layer neural circuit with four neuron types (resource, point, map, and goal cells) using biologically realistic structures and learning rules. The circuit learns environmental topology through Hebbian plasticity in map cell synapses, and goal cells produce signals that decline systematically with distance from target locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C18 collectively describe the circuit architecture and its key functional property. The mathematical formulations (Equations 1-18), detailed circuit diagrams (Figure 1B), and simulation results (Figures 2-5) provide strong converging evidence that this circuit can implement the proposed functions using local learning rules.

results.result: Map cells learn the connectivity structure of the environment through Hebbian strengthening of recurrent synapses when the animal moves between adjacent locations, causing the synaptic weight matrix to converge to the adjacency matrix of the environment graph.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 describe the map learning mechanism with support from mathematical theory (Equations 1-5), citations to established learning theory (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Galtier et al., 2012), and simulation demonstrations (Figure 2, Figure 4B). The convergence to the adjacency matrix is both theoretically predicted and empirically demonstrated.

results.result: The goal signal computed by the endotaxis network declines monotonically with graph distance from the target, allowing an agent to navigate the shortest path by making local decisions that maximize the goal signal at each step without high-level planning.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C53-C55 describe the core navigation principle. This is supported by mathematical derivations (Equations 10-17 showing exponential decay with distance), theoretical analysis proving monotonic distance dependence for appropriate parameters, and extensive simulations (Figures 3-5) demonstrating successful shortest-path navigation across diverse graph structures.

results.result: At a noise level of ε=0.01, endotaxis enables perfect navigation over distances of approximately 9 steps across diverse graph structures (ring, binary tree, Tower of Hanoi), providing 10-100× speedup compared to random navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C60-C63 report quantitative performance metrics from simulations. Figure 5 provides comprehensive data across three different graph types, showing consistent navigation range of ~9 steps and quantified speedup factors. The consistency across structurally different environments strengthens the claim of generality.

results.result: The endotaxis model requires parameter tuning but is relatively robust, allowing 10-20% variation in parameters for reasonable performance, though the exponential decay of goal signals presents challenges for biological implementation due to finite neuronal signal-to-noise ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C56-C57 address practical implementation constraints. Figure 6 systematically explores parameter sensitivity across three graph types, demonstrating the claimed 10-20% tolerance. The biological constraint discussion (C56-C57) is grounded in established neuroscience knowledge about discrimination thresholds (~1%) and provides context for the noise levels used in simulations.

results.result: A saturating nonlinear activation function in map neurons improves navigation performance by 1.5-2.2× compared to linear activation, by maintaining constant peak map output which has a normalizing effect that prevents learning errors and local maxima in the goal signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C28 and C67 describe an enhancement to the basic model. Figure 7 provides quantitative comparisons showing the performance improvements, mechanistic explanations for why saturation helps (Figure 7E-F), and demonstrates the effect across multiple graph types. The explanation linking normalization to improved performance is well-supported.

results.result: Endotaxis can explain the observed homing behavior in mice that navigate back to a labyrinth entrance using the shortest path on their first visit, without retracing their exploratory route.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C69 connect model predictions to experimental observations. The experimental data from Rosenberg et al., 2021 (C29) establishes the phenomenon. Figure 8 demonstrates that the endotaxis model with partially learned maps produces goal signals that enable correct homing behavior, including the specific prediction that agents turn toward shortcuts rather than retracing steps (C69).

results.result: Real mice spend >85% of their time patrolling a learned maze with efficiency between random and optimal, continuing for hours after perfecting navigation to reward locations. The optimal patrol path for the binary tree maze visits all 64 end nodes in 252 steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C70-C71 report experimental observations from Rosenberg et al., 2021. The optimal path calculation (C31) is a computational result shown in Figure 9A. The mouse behavior data (C32, C70-C71) comes from the cited experimental study and is quantified in Figure 9B, providing empirical grounding for the patrolling phenomenon the model aims to explain.

results.result: Endotaxis with habituation in point cells can implement efficient patrolling behavior, with performance at noise level ε≈1 matching the efficiency of real mice, which is intermediate between random and optimal patrolling.
results.evaluation: The model extension with habituation (Algorithm 3) produces patrolling behavior demonstrated in Figure 9. At ε=0.01, the model achieves perfect patrolling (Figure 9A), while at ε≈1 it matches mouse behavior (Figure 9B). The mechanism is clearly specified and the match to experimental data is quantitative, though the habituation parameters (β=1.2, τ=100) appear to be fitted to produce this match.

results.result: Endotaxis operates continuously with the same learning rules during exploration, navigation, and patrolling, integrating latent learning (map acquisition without rewards) and reinforcement learning (goal tagging), enabling navigation to goal locations after a single reinforcement.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C80-C83 describe the unified learning framework. Figure 4 demonstrates one-shot goal learning after map acquisition. The integration of latent and reinforcement learning is supported by the mathematical formulation (Equation 18) showing goal signals depend on both map and goal synapses. The historical context (C81-C82) and distinction from prior models strengthens the conceptual claim.

results.result: The mushroom body of arthropod brains contains neural circuit elements analogous to the endotaxis model: Kenyon cells with sparse responses and strong recurrent connections (map cells), output neurons with reward-gated plasticity (goal cells), and connections to turning control circuits, potentially supporting odor-landmark navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 propose biological correspondence between the model and insect brain structures. While each anatomical claim is supported by appropriate citations (Heisenberg 2003, Eichler et al. 2017, Cohn et al. 2015, etc.), the functional interpretation that these structures implement endotaxis (C40) is speculative. The citations support the existence of the structures and some of their properties, but not their specific role in the proposed navigation algorithm.

results.result: Rodent hippocampal place cells show properties consistent with endotaxis predictions: rapid appearance of place fields upon entering new environments, sparse activation of potential place cells, goal cells with large place fields, and sudden formation of fully-formed place fields triggered by dendritic calcium plateaus with multi-second plasticity windows.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 connect model predictions to mammalian neuroscience. Each claim is supported by specific citations to experimental studies (Wilson & McNaughton 1993, Alme et al. 2014, Hok et al. 2005, Bittner et al. 2017, Magee & Grienberger 2020). The correspondence between model predictions and experimental observations is clearly articulated, though the claims are correlational rather than demonstrating that these neurons actually implement endotaxis.

results.result: Endotaxis can be viewed as a form of reinforcement learning that differs from standard approaches and the successor representation by: (1) having no time/reward tradeoff and seeking only shortest paths, (2) externalizing action selection to the environment, and (3) learning only state functions rather than state-action value functions, which simplifies the circuit at the cost of limiting planning capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C84, C87, C89-C92 position endotaxis within reinforcement learning theory. The comparisons are conceptually clear and supported by appropriate citations (Sutton & Barto 2018, Dayan 1993, Stachenfeld et al. 2017). The distinctions are well-articulated and follow logically from the model architecture. However, the evaluation is primarily conceptual/theoretical rather than empirically validated through direct comparisons.

results.result: Endotaxis distinguishes itself from prior navigation models by using forward signal propagation from current location (rather than backward from goal), having goal neurons that also respond to resources directly, operating continuously without separating learning and navigation phases, and covering all essential functions in a feed-forward neuromorphically plausible manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C100 compare endotaxis to prior computational models. The review of prior approaches is well-cited (Gaussier et al. 2002, Ponulak & Hopfield 2013, etc.). The distinctions claimed for endotaxis (C95-C96, C97-C98, C100) follow logically from the model architecture described earlier. The claim of being more complete and biologically plausible (C100) is somewhat subjective but reasonably supported by the detailed circuit specification and learning rules.

results.result: Chemotaxis is universal among motile animals, always includes trial-and-error search strategies, and may have been the original evolutionary driver for brain development, with ancient brain regions like the hippocampus organized around olfactory processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 provide evolutionary and behavioral context. C4 and C7 are supported by Baker et al. 2018. C5 is presented as a belief in the field (knowledge claim). C6 is supported by Jacobs 2012 and Aboitiz & Montiel 2015. These are background claims that motivate the model but are not central results of this work. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Animals navigate using real-world trial-and-error, especially during early learning, as evidenced by vicarious trial-and-error behaviors (head swaying at decision points) observed across species from insects to humans, which may represent sampling of internal virtual odor gradients in endotaxis.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50, C75-C76 connect the model's trial-and-error mechanism to animal behavior. The behavioral observations are well-cited (Redish 2016, Lashley 1912, Tarsitano 2006, Santos-Pata & Verschure 2018). The interpretation that these behaviors reflect sampling of virtual odors (implied connection to endotaxis) is more speculative but follows logically from the model. The evidence supports that trial-and-error occurs but not definitively that it implements endotaxis.

results.result: Animals entering new environments face challenges of exploration, memorization, and navigation. Endotaxis provides a brain module solution using neural components found across species from insects to humans, interfacing between spatial sensing and chemotaxis modules.
results.evaluation: C1 is a general framing claim about animal behavior (knowledge-based). C3 and C47 propose that endotaxis components exist across species and could serve as an interface module. C3 is supported by the Discussion section's review of insect and mammalian neuroscience. C47 is more speculative about the modular architecture. These are primarily framing and interpretive claims rather than empirical results.

results.result: The ~9 step navigation range of endotaxis at ε=0.01 is ecologically relevant, as personal experience suggests humans rarely learn routes with more than 9 successive decisions, and chess openings typically last about 10 moves.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 attempt to validate the model's performance range by comparison to human behavior. C64 is explicitly based on informal personal experience (speculation). C65 about chess openings is factual (knowledge) but the connection to spatial navigation is tenuous. These claims lack rigorous empirical support and the analogies may not be appropriate. The ecological relevance argument is weak.

results.result: Mice can navigate novel direct routes through a labyrinth on first attempt and spend most waking time patrolling even after perfecting routes to rewards.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 report experimental observations from Rosenberg et al., 2021. These are empirical findings from a prior study that motivate the current modeling work. The claims are appropriately cited and provide the behavioral phenomena that the endotaxis model aims to explain. These are not results of the current manuscript but important context.

results.result: Endotaxis does not implement advanced spatial reasoning capabilities such as action chunking or internal deliberation for route planning.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 explicitly acknowledges limitations of the model. This is an honest assessment of what the model does not do, which is important for scientific clarity. The limitation follows logically from the model architecture which makes only local decisions. This is a straightforward descriptive claim about model scope.

results.result: The endotaxis model consists of a 3-layer neural circuit with four cell types (resource, point, map, and goal cells) that uses biologically plausible Hebbian learning rules to learn environmental structure and generate distance-dependent goal signals for navigation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently describe the model architecture positively. Reviewer 2 provides a detailed summary of the model mechanics without criticism, stating 'the ideas are interesting and the presentation of the results in the manuscript is generally clear.' Reviewer 1 notes the model is 'highly compelling' and 'well-written.' The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing.' No reviewer challenges the basic architecture or learning mechanisms.

results.result: The endotaxis network computes shortest graph distances such that goal cell activity declines systematically with distance from the target, enabling navigation by local gradient ascent without high-level planning.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms this mechanism: 'after learning the activity of goal cells decreases exponentially with the diffusion distance from the corresponding goal location. The organism can therefore navigate to a given goal by doing gradient ascent.' Reviewer 1 states the model 'performed reasonably well' and calls it 'very compelling.' No reviewer disputes the core computational principle.

results.result: Simulations demonstrate that endotaxis enables navigation over ~9 steps at 1% noise, functions across diverse graph structures (ring, tree, Tower of Hanoi), and dramatically outperforms random navigation (40-100x faster), with parameter tuning requirements that are generous (10-20% tolerance).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly validates these results: 'They show (1) in practical terms, the spreading signal travels further for a larger decay but becomes erratic as the decay parameter approaches its theoretical upper bound... it is perhaps helpful to see that there is a viable range of values... (2) That different graph structures can be acquired and used to approach goal locations.' Reviewer 1 confirms 'the Endotaxis model performed reasonably well across different environments.' The quantitative performance claims are not challenged.

results.result: A saturating activation function increases navigation range by factors of 1.5-2.2 across different graphs through a normalizing effect that keeps peak map output constant.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 acknowledges this finding without criticism, noting the results show 'the parameters interact in expected ways.' The specific quantitative improvements are presented in the manuscript data (Figure 7) and not disputed by any reviewer.

results.result: Endotaxis can explain mouse homing behavior where animals navigate directly to the entrance on first visit without retracing their path, as demonstrated in simulations matching experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 acknowledges this application: 'the separation of goals from states can be used flexibly e.g. the homing behaviour (a goal state is learned before any of the map is learned).' The experimental observation from Rosenberg et al. 2021 is cited and the simulation result is not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Real mice spend >85% of time patrolling mazes even after perfecting navigation, with efficiency between random and optimal; endotaxis can generate similar patrolling behavior.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly notes this result: 'the patrolling behaviour (a goal cell that monitors all states for how recently they were visited).' The experimental observations from Rosenberg et al. 2021 are cited and the model's ability to account for this behavior is not disputed.

results.result: The mushroom body in arthropods contains circuit elements (Kenyon cells, recurrent connectivity, reward-gated plasticity, output neurons guiding turning) that resemble the endotaxis architecture, suggesting insects may use odors as navigational landmarks.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 raises significant concerns: 'it goes substantially beyond any available evidence to claim that KC connectivity could support the acquisition of a graph (in the form of an adjacency matrix) representing the structure of the environment: KCs show sparse distributed activity (not one active node per state); it seems unlikely that any two arbitrary KCs can (rapidly) become connected; and as yet has not been demonstrated that KC connectivity is plastic at all.' This directly challenges the biological plausibility of the insect mapping despite the cited anatomical similarities.

results.result: Hippocampal place cells appear rapidly upon environment entry, with only a fraction active in any environment; goal-like cells exist in rat cortex; place fields can appear suddenly via dendritic plateau potentials; and plasticity mechanisms extend over several seconds—all consistent with endotaxis predictions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the discussion 'focussed exclusively on the hippocampus without any link to olfaction, which feels like a missed opportunity' and suggests the olfactory tubercle as a more appropriate mapping. Reviewer 3 also states 'I was also surprised not to see any discussion of internally generated sequential activity in the hippocampus as a possible mechanism for the look-ahead needed to evaluate the goal distance gradient.' These comments indicate the hippocampal mapping is incomplete and potentially missing key mechanisms.

results.result: Endotaxis resembles the successor representation but differs by using policy-independent adjacency matrices rather than policy-dependent transitions, externalizing action selection, and learning only scalar state functions rather than state-action values.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 extensively discusses this relationship and notes 'there are several prior proposals for policy-independent SR-like mechanisms that it would be useful to discuss,' citing Baram et al., Kaelbling, Piray and Daw, and Fang et al. The editor also notes 'the relationship to existing similar hypotheses could be clarified.' This indicates the claimed distinctions from prior work need better contextualization.

results.result: Endotaxis distinguishes itself from prior navigation models by using forward signal propagation from current location, reading out at the goal location, operating continuously without separate learning/navigation phases, and covering all essential functions in a feed-forward neuromorphically plausible manner.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 acknowledges these claimed advantages but notes 'the approach relates closely to previous models of exploration, learning, and navigation' and that 'many of these similarly claim to be plausible neural circuits.' Reviewer 3's extensive discussion of related work (SR, Baram et al., etc.) and the editor's note that 'the relationship to existing similar hypotheses could be clarified' suggest the distinctiveness claims need better support.

results.result: Endotaxis operates continuously ('always on') without separating learning and navigation phases, integrates latent learning and reinforcement learning, enables one-shot learning from single reinforcement, and relies fundamentally on trial-and-error rather than deliberative planning.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly acknowledges this feature: 'does not require any separate control or rules for learning vs. navigation phases' and notes this as a 'desirable feature.' Reviewer 1 confirms the model is 'compelling from an evolutionary perspective and a mechanistic perspective.' The continuous operation and integration of learning types are not challenged.

results.result: Chemotaxis is universal across animals, brains evolved to organize motor responses to chemical stimuli, ancient brain regions like hippocampus are organized around olfactory processing, and trial-and-error navigation with vicarious trial and error behaviors occurs across species from insects to humans.
results.evaluation: These background claims are well-cited and not disputed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 calls the chemotaxis framing 'compelling from an evolutionary perspective.' Reviewer 3 notes this is 'an interesting and attractive aspect of the work' though suggests the olfactory connection could be developed further in the discussion.

results.result: Experimental observations from Rosenberg et al. 2021 show mice can navigate novel labyrinths using direct routes on first attempt and spend most time patrolling even after learning.
results.evaluation: These are cited experimental observations that reviewers accept. Reviewer 4 acknowledges the model's ability to account for these behaviors. No reviewer questions the validity of the experimental findings.

results.result: Endotaxis represents a brain module that could be interposed between spatial-sensing and taxis modules.
results.evaluation: This conceptual framing is accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 1 states 'this framework will likely be very important for understanding how the hippocampus (and other memory/navigation-related circuits) interfaces with other processes in the brain.' The modular architecture concept is not challenged.

results.result: Personal experience and chess openings suggest humans rarely learn routes involving more than 9-10 successive decisions.
results.evaluation: These informal observations are presented as context for the ~9 step navigation range and are not disputed by reviewers. They serve as supporting context rather than primary claims.
